title: The Model Is the Refinery; the Value Is in the Chemical Plants and the Car Companies
dek: In business history, the companies that broke out in the first wave are almost never the winners of the next stage. Model companies are refineries that distill base oil; the real money is in the application layer that wires intelligence into the workflows of banks, pharma and government.
why: Levie breaks the "application layer vs. model layer" bet into concrete mechanisms: why subsidies must end, where open weights win, and why coding diffuses fast while other knowledge work is slow.
who: Founders building enterprise software and AI applications, investors betting on the application layer, and CTOs agonising over whether they should train their own models.
skip: The opening jokes about root canals and Doug Leone, roughly 0:30 to 1:55.

points.h: Between the model and the workflow lies a trillion-dollar gap
points.body: Levie says the market's past two years of dismissing the "model wrapper" were wrong, because what enterprises actually need is the bridge from model capability to real workflows. That bridge is either very limited or very large — roughly a trillion dollars is riding on which of those two outcomes it is. He judges the bridge is obviously large: however smart the model, the workflow still has to connect to other data systems, keep a human in the loop, wait on latency, and deal with legacy systems. Those five to ten things are all operational grunt work, and research organisations are the last people who want to do them.

points.h: The infrastructure-and-applications script has already been played once
points.body: Levie uses the cloud analogy to rebut "models will eat everything": AWS, GCP and Azure created trillions in market cap, but there is also trillions in software value that exists only because of them. He says that if you had looked ten years ago at what AWS and GCP were building, you would never have predicted Snowflake or Databricks would appear — you would have thought the infrastructure already did these things, so why would anyone pay ten billion dollars of revenue for a product that "just lets you process data". Intelligence will take the same path: models will be enormously valuable, but bringing models into the workflows of banking, life sciences, healthcare and government is itself a great deal of software.

points.h: Subsidising tokens cannot go on forever
points.body: Levie thinks "the fox guarding the henhouse" is the structural reason the application layer must exist: when you hand a task to an agent system, you want the cost optimised with accuracy unchanged, which by definition should be done by a company that does not care which model is used. The countervailing force is that model companies can subsidise their own models, but he judges that cannot last — once these companies go public they will be bound by the same laws of capitalism; and the subsidies may already have crossed a threshold once they reached the scale of tens of billions in capex, and in the end they still have to pay for training runs. He adds an equilibrium problem: if the API is a high-margin business subsidising the application product, and all the customers get migrated onto the application product, the API revenue is gone.

points.h: Code is a tool; content is a proxy for character
points.body: Levie splits apart the difference in tolerance for "work slop": for most people in the world, code is a utility, it is just about automating something or letting someone press a button to get to the next step, so having an agent generate an entire backend or frontend is not only acceptable but preferable. Content is different — when you receive a deck, you are still judging "can I trust this person to execute on this", and work slop destroys that judgement. He admits he uses AI for brainstorming himself, but when he receives someone else's AI output he is equally suspicious; it is a collective trap, and it may take three to five years to get through it.

points.h: Open-weight adoption is higher than people think, lower than enterprises want
points.body: Levie gives a three-part judgement: open-weight adoption in enterprises is "higher than people think, lower than enterprises actually want, and much lower than it will be in five years". He estimates that 30% or more of it is attributable to the novelty of "wanting to try GLM" rather than cost — he has seen Fortune 500 CIOs say they are playing with open source, but he knows that at that cost tier Gemini or Muse would have been good enough anyway. The current practical obstacles are concrete: sometimes token efficiency is lower, sometimes it randomly starts speaking Chinese in the middle of a chain, which is very strange for a bank. In the long run, mature use cases will be peeled off onto open weights, provided it really is cheaper, or post-training can deliver extra performance.

points.h: Burning context into the weights runs into the enterprise permissions wall
points.body: Levie is interested in continual learning, but points out that the real friction in the enterprise world is permissions and access control. He says researchers often imagine the world runs their way — I have full access, so a model trained only in my world would be great — but a lawyer has an extremely small access point of five projects, because a colleague one door down is working on a competitor's project, and no document can pass between the two; it has to be a hard partition. Even if you could train a model for a single user, what about the fact that this person is added to or removed from projects every day, bringing in new and important context. He thinks this only gets really interesting once the cost curve comes down and open weights get smaller and faster.

points.h: A system of record must do both ends; doing one end loses
points.body: Levie says that if you are a SaaS platform with data and customer workflows, there are two things you must do at the same time, and doing only one means you lose. First, you have to have an agent that is absurdly strong on your own product, provably 10 to 20 points better than a general agent, not by crippling the competition but by maxing out evals and tuning for the workflow. Second, you must be headless, exposing APIs to Claude, ChatGPT and every other platform, letting external agents call you through MCP or deterministic APIs. He gives his own example: because he can get into Salesforce through Claude or ChatGPT MCP, he now uses Salesforce roughly ten times as often as before.

points.h: Coding diffuses fast because it hits all six conditions
points.body: Levie lists six properties of why coding got out first: the value of code is almost 100% represented by the generated text; models are trained on vast amounts of code; every AI lab treats coding as a competitive benchmark and runs its own evals every day; the users are the most technical population in history, so when they hit a bug or an MCP connection failure they fix it themselves instead of calling; and it is a high-paying vertical, so a 10% to 20% productivity gain automatically has value. By contrast, a sales rep's value creation is persuading an external customer to buy software or a Caterpillar truck, constrained by whether the customer replies, whether there is budget, whether they can meet next Tuesday — this is a continuum between "rate-limited by external factors" and "able to sit at a computer and type all day".

The engineering layer that wraps a model, wires in search and the file system, and orchestrates multi-step retrieval and reranking.
The direction of letting model weights continuously adapt to a specific user or organisation through use, rather than relying only on context retrieval.
A model whose weights are publicly downloadable and deployable, so enterprises can host it themselves to push down inference costs.
A protocol that lets external agents call a given system's API in a standard way.
